The bell above the door of "Cog & Sprocket – Repairs & Oddities" chimed a discordant, rusty melody as Ruth pushed it open, a nervous flutter in her stomach mimicking the sound. The air inside was thick with the scent of oil, metal shavings, and something vaguely floral, like potpourri someone had forgotten about years ago. It was a surprisingly pleasant combination, though, a comforting aroma of industry and quiet resilience. Sunlight struggled to penetrate the grime-coated windows, casting the space in a perpetual twilight.

The shop itself was a glorious chaos. Shelves overflowed with spare parts – gears of every conceivable size, springs coiled like sleeping snakes, lengths of wire tangled into nests. Tools hung from pegboards in a haphazard, yet somehow organized, fashion. Antique clocks with missing hands leaned against grandfather clocks in need of serious attention. A taxidermied badger, wearing a tiny waistcoat, sat perched atop a pile of disassembled radios. It was a far cry from the neat, predictable world Ruth had known.

She’d answered an ad tacked to the community board at the library: “Apprentice Needed – Cog & Sprocket. Must be willing to learn, and not afraid of grease.” Willing to learn was an understatement. Ruth, fresh out of a series of dead-end office jobs, was desperate to learn *anything* that involved tangible creation, something that left her with a feeling of accomplishment beyond spreadsheets and staplers. And she wasn’t afraid of grease. She was, in fact, rather looking forward to it.

Behind a workbench piled high with disassembled cuckoo clocks, a man looked up. He was older, with a face etched with the stories of countless repairs, and hands that moved with the practiced ease of someone who’d spent a lifetime manipulating tiny mechanisms. His hair was a salt-and-pepper tangle escaping from beneath a leather cap, and a pair of spectacles perched precariously on his nose. He didn't smile, but his eyes, magnified by the lenses, held a flicker of something…curious?

“You’re the…applicant?” he asked, his voice raspy, like a well-worn gear.

Ruth swallowed, suddenly feeling very young and awkward in her sensible shoes and neatly pressed dress. "Yes, sir. Ruth Albright." She extended her hand, and he briefly, almost reluctantly, shook it, his grip surprisingly firm.

“Mr. Silas Blackwood,” he replied, returning to his work. He picked up a minuscule screwdriver and began meticulously adjusting a tiny lever within the clockwork. “So. You want to learn how things work?” He didn’t look up, but Ruth felt the question directed squarely at her. “It’s not all gleaming brass and happy chimes, you know. There's a lot of frustration. A lot of tiny screws. A lot of things that break in ways you wouldn't think possible.” 



He paused, finally meeting her gaze over the rim of his spectacles. "Tell me," he said, his voice quieter now, “what do you know about escapements?”
